evidence: Caes. BC 2.15.2: māteriae, of timber (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of the body, of health, and of anything that lacks strength, and so helplessness; weak is imbēcillus (Cic. Amic. 23: imbēcillī valent, the weak are strong). A weak point in a person or an argument is a vitium.

terms.gloss: lack of strength, weakness; in later Latin, illness
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.1: summa gracilitās et īnfirmitās corporis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of children, of the body, of a building; from Pliny and Suetonius on also sickness, indisposition (Lewis & Short). Weak is īnfirmus.

phrases.latin: Tulliae meae morbus et imbēcillitās corporis mē exanimat
phrases.english: my Tullia’s illness and physical weakness are killing me with worry

phrases.latin: ut et īnfirmitās puerōrum et ferōcitās juvenum et gravitās jam cōnstantis aetātis et senectūtis mātūritās nātūrāle quiddam habeat, quod suō tempore percipī dēbeat
phrases.english: so that the weakness of children, the fire of the young, the gravity of settled middle age and the ripeness of old age each have something natural about them, to be gathered in its own season

sources: Lewis & Short: imbecillitas · Lewis & Short: imbecillus · Lewis & Short: infirmitas
